newsitem.title: IRAN: Iran sees no thaw in ties till U.S. ends hostility.
newsitem.headline: Iran sees no thaw in ties till U.S. ends hostility.

text.p: Iran sees no quick change in its confrontation with the United States after the re-election of President Bill Clinton.
But, while hardliners reject any possibility of reconciliation, increasingly others link a thaw to Washington dropping its hostility toward the Islamic republic.

"So long as the U.S. pursues the strategy of aggression, our foreign policy regarding the United States will remain unchanged," Deputy Speaker of Parliament Hassan Rowhani said in remarks published on Thursday.

"Clinton at the start of his first term of presidency commissioned a group to survey U.S. foreign policy. He should demand a similar revision at the start of his second term," Rowhani, who is also the secretary of Iran's National Security Council, told the English-language daily Iran News.

The United States imposed a trade and investment ban on Iran in June 1995, accusing it of sponsoring terrorism and seeking to develop nuclear weapons. Iran denies the charges and says the United States is bent on destroying the Islamic government.

Washington stepped up its campaign to isolate Tehran last August, threatening to use a new law that tightened sanctions against non-U.S. firms who invest at least $40 million in Iran's vital oil and gas industry.
Iran's United Nations ambassador Kamal Kharrazi on Tuesday said no dialogue with Washington was possible at this time.
"Washington should first show goodwill and as a prerequisite must prove its readiness to abandon its hegemonic and arrogant attitude," Kharrazi told the official news agency IRNA.
Iranian state radio said on Wednesday Clinton's re-election meant the United States would maintain its "interventionist and arrogant" policies.

Last week Resalat newspaper said there were two camps among Iran's leaders: one that saw a thaw with Washington possible if conditions were met, and another that rejected any improvement in ties with the "Great Satan," as the United States is often called in Iran.
The newspaper suggested Iran's supreme leader Ayatollah Khamenei belonged to the second camp.

Khamenei last week rejected suggestions talks could be held with Washington. He was apparently referring to a call by U.S. Assistant Secretary of State Robert Pelletreau for talks with Tehran on bilateral differences.
But President Akbar Hashemi Rafsanjani said Tehran's policy since the time of the late spiritual leader Ayatollah Khomeini had been to demand an end to Washington's anti-Iran stand.

"It is America's own fault. If they calm down, as the Imam (Khomeini) put it, there are no problems from our side. The leader's (Khamenei's) present policy is the same and I also follow this line," Rafsanjani told the daily Iran on Monday.
An Iranian analyst said Tehran leaders would see it as weakness to have contacts while Washington wages a world campaign against it.

"The Iranians have a long list of grievances to be addressed by the U.S. They basically think the ball, as far as any moves towards improvements are concerned, is in the U.S. court," the analyst said.

Washington broke diplomatic ties with Tehran in 1980 after Moslem militants seized the U.S. embassy there, holding 52 Americans hostage for 444 days in the wake of the Islamic revolution that toppled the late shah, a close U.S. ally.
